expectations.text: The inline proposal is written to a file before the debate so every role argues against the same fixed text
expectations.evidence: work/pytest-migration-proposal.md contains the user's prompt verbatim plus a structured restatement (Position, 3 arguments for, 3 downsides). The debate transcript header names it as the Artifact: '**Artifact:** .../work/pytest-migration-proposal.md'. user_notes.md item 1: 'I wrote the request's inline proposal verbatim (plus a structured restatement) to work/pytest-migration-proposal.md before Phase 1.' Roles then argue against that fixed text; e.g., the Judge's Ruling 1 checks it directly: 'I checked the artifact. It is 26 lines, it lists "6,000 existing tests" as an unmitigated downside, and it contains no affordability claim.'

expectations.text: The pro side argues with the user's specifics (fixtures vs setUp inheritance, parametrize vs copy-paste, xdist parallelism)
expectations.evidence: Defender Phase 1 presents all three verbatim arguments with mechanism ('pytest fixtures are named, composable, request-scoped dependencies', '@pytest.mark.parametrize collapses those into one test body with a table of cases', 'pytest-xdist distributes tests across CPU cores with a command-line flag'). The Advocate's Phase 4 case deepens each: point 3 makes fixtures-vs-setUp a monorepo ownership argument ('conftest.py resolves by directory, which maps onto monorepo ownership boundaries'), point 5 details parametrize vs copy-paste ('adding a case is a one-line diff to a table. Under copy-paste, it is a new method'), point 4 defends xdist including '--dist loadfile' graceful degradation.

expectations.text: The con side engages the real costs (6k-test migration, CI churn, team familiarity), not strawmen
expectations.evidence: Adversary Objection 1 engages the 6k-test cost precisely: parametrize and argument-injected fixtures do not work on TestCase methods, so 'in the cheap scope... arguments 1 and 2 deliver zero value against the existing 6,000 tests'. Objections 2 and 3 engage CI churn concretely (parallel-safety unknown, silent collection loss via load_tests/custom TestResult, dual-runner CI overlap). Objection 5 goes beyond the stated familiarity cost rather than strawmanning it: 'The proposal lists "some devs know unittest well" as the human downside. That is the weakest version of the real cost... the actual cost is... two test idioms simultaneously, for a duration the proposal does not bound.' The Adversary also concedes points where the pro side is right (subTest vs parametrize, ecosystem argument), which is the opposite of strawmanning.

expectations.text: The review surfaces that pytest runs existing unittest tests, enabling incremental migration instead of a rewrite
expectations.evidence: Defender Phase 1 (transcript line 27): 'pytest runs unittest.TestCase suites natively. Switching the runner does not require rewriting the 6k tests up front.' Advocate point 2: 'The 6,000 tests are an inventory to convert opportunistically, not a bill due at migration time.' The compatibility limits are also mapped (Phase 3, Advocate Q2: load_tests ignored, no parametrize on TestCase methods). The final answer.md carries it to the user: 'The two arguments that emerged strongest were ones you did not make: the asymmetry (pytest runs unittest.TestCase natively...)' and the agreed scope sentence 'adopt pytest as the runner now; convert TestCase files only when already modifying them'.

expectations.text: A debate transcript shows distinct role contributions: opening case, objections, defense, rebuttal, and a judge assessment
expectations.evidence: outputs/transcript.md is structured by phase and role: 'Phase 1 — Defender: Opening Statement'; Phase 2 clarifying questions from Adversary and Advocate; Phase 3 Defender's answers (defense of the artifact's claims, conceding unknowns); Phase 4 'Adversary's case' (Objections 1-5) and 'Advocate's case' (points 1-8); Phase 5 'Adversary's rebuttal' and 'Advocate's rebuttal'; Phase 6 'Judge's Final Report' with Agreed changes, Dropped objections, Contested points, Rulings 1-8, and a recommendation. The contributions are substantively distinct (roles concede to each other, cite each other's phase text, and disagree in the rulings), not one voice relabeled.

expectations.text: The output ends with a recommendation and explicitly leaves the final decision to the user
expectations.evidence: answer.md states the recommendation ('The Judge recommends approving the switch, with preconditions', 'My read matches the Judge: Option 1') and opens with 'You get final say.' Its closing section is titled 'Your decision' and lists Options 1-4 for the user to choose. The Judge's report in the transcript likewise ends with a 'Your decision' section presenting four options rather than deciding.

claims.claim: pytest does not respect the load_tests protocol, bypasses custom TestRunner/TestResult subclasses, parametrize does not work on TestCase methods, and fixtures cannot be argument-injected into TestCase methods
claims.evidence: Matches pytest's documented unittest integration. These facts are load-bearing for Objection 3 and the collection-parity gate, and they are stated accurately.

claims.claim: unittest has had -k since Python 3.7 and --failfast for longer; coverage.py runs unittest via 'coverage run -m unittest'; unittest-xml-reporting provides JUnit XML
claims.evidence: All correct. The Judge additionally corrected the Adversary's '-k: not a delta' overstatement (pytest -k supports boolean expressions, unittest -k substring/glob patterns), which is also accurate.

claims.claim: A session-scoped fixture runs once per xdist worker, so sharing one external resource across workers requires lock coordination
claims.evidence: Correct; each xdist worker is a separate process, and the pytest-xdist docs describe the file-lock pattern for once-per-session resources.

claims.claim: The Judge checked the artifact directly: 'It is 26 lines... and it contains no affordability claim. The affordability fact appears only at transcript line 27'
claims.evidence: work/pytest-migration-proposal.md is 26 lines and contains no compatibility/affordability claim. suggestions.reason: No expectation checks role isolation, which is the skill's core mechanism: the fresh-eyes Adversary and Advocate should be separate subagents that see only the artifact and transcript, not the coordinator's context. This run did it correctly (7 Agent calls, read-only Explore subagents per user_notes), but a run where one writer roleplays all four voices in a single context would pass every current assertion. Consider an assertion like 'the Adversary and Advocate roles run as separate fresh-context subagents, evidenced by Agent tool calls in the execution log'.

No expectation checks the technical accuracy of the debate's load-bearing facts (pytest's unittest-compatibility limits: load_tests ignored, no parametrize on TestCase methods). This run got them right and the entire Objection 1/3 structure depends on them; a debate built on a wrong compatibility claim would still satisfy all six assertions. A spot-check assertion on one named compatibility fact would make the eval discriminate on correctness, not just structure.

eval_feedback.overall: The six assertions are well-chosen and discriminating for debate structure and content fidelity; this run passes all of them with strong evidence. The two gaps are mechanism (role isolation) and factual accuracy of the pytest claims the debate turns on.
